review:
[b]Duke Nukem?[/b]

Not exactly, but Sam "Serious" Stone has similarly funny one-liners (albeit much fewer) when he blows up an alien attempting to kill him. In the cutscenes you can also notice he is full of muscles and that he also wears sunglasses. This was Croteam's own hero with which they wanted to conquer the FPS genre back in 2001.

[b]So what is this?[/b]

The idea was to tone down the gameplay we got to know in Duke Nukem. Duke could use some items which were strategically important at select locations. Also, we frequently searched for objects such as keycards. And remember that heights also became important? That with our jetpack secrets became accessible?

Sam makes it way simpler: he shoots first then asks questions later. We go from one room to another and only when we killed everybody can we proceed. Sometimes we have to activate levers but these are rare occasions. With Sam it really is all about shooting and increasing our score for each level. Greater difficulty settings yield us increased multipliers. We do not even have to reload our weapons (a similarity with Doom).

[b]Story? Is there such a thing?[/b]

Well, yes. We hunt for artifacts in Egypt (sometime in the future) to make sure we can kill the leader of the enemy race invading Earth. We know we failed but Sam was able to use a special device to travel back in time to correct our mistake. Although  the entire first game takes place in Egypt the locales vary from tombs and city-like areas to deserts and at one point we even find ourselves in the sewers. Don't expect an interesting story and dozens of cutscenes here, though.

[b]A new, more serious version[/b]

The 3rd iteration of Croteam's Serious Engine was used to completely redo the original game. Screenshots and comparison videos speak for themselves: the game has better looking, crispier textures and each alien was completely remodelled to look better. A later version of the engine was used to make the 3rd episode in the series. It does its job properly without changing the core gameplay which is just as fast and dynamic as it was in the original version.

[b]A serious purchase[/b]

This is how you remaster your software. You make it look better, sound louder and neglect annoying DLCs (I am looking at you, Painkiller). If you are a newcomer to this franchise perhaps Serious Sam 3 should be your first purchase (after all, it is a prequel to the story). However, if you played this 15 years ago when you were a kid it's high time you included it in your library of digital games.

Out of all the classic style FPSes, This is one of them. Ridiculous, outrageous, and punishing.

When you find a Secret in any other FPS game, you're usually treated to a nice little boost of health, maybe a new gun or a power up, or maybe just ammo.

In Serious Sam, the secret is +1 armor and when you pick it up the game grabs you by the lapels and screams "HOW DARE YOU" in your face and demands you explain yourself to the 410,757,864,530 Kleer skeletons that just spawned in the bathroom stall sized room you're in.

Secret levels are the same way. You'll walk in from the last level shoving your appendix back inside your gut, get full health and ammo, and leave clutching your appendix yet again after getting mauled by harpies and Swiss cheesed by mechanoids, all while trying to shoot Kamikazes and avoid entire family reunion of Gnaars. 

Playing Serious Sam is like headbutting trees: Its fun, but you're going to get a traumatic brain injury if you do it too much. 

Take breaks and drink plenty of water. Give your mom a call and ask her about her day after you've died to the same area for the 30th time in the past hour. Take a walk and listen to the birds and take in some nature.

I rate it "Cock and Ball Torture: The Game"/10

Serious Sam is great thanks in large part to its deceptive simplicity.

Sure, Sam is a character meant to parody the muscle-bound, shoot first, unstoppable action heroes that embodied the early FPS era. But what's great about Sam is that his game takes itself very serious, when it has every right not to.

The original Serious Sam: TFE, and this HD release, have a lot of heart. You can tell there was a clear vision behind this Croteam release, and while the game isn't revolutionary by any sense of the word, it is damn fun. The gameplay loop is simple, but the game puts enough of a spin on it to keep it fresh. You're going to spend your time running away from an insane amount of enemies--it's a horde shooter after all--but what's great is each enemy has a clear weakness. 

That's the deceptive part about Serious Sam. On the surface, you're just fighting a bunch of enemies who are mostly just cannon fodder. But once you understand the game's intricacies: weapons that work well on certain enemies, using enemies against each other, how to dodge attacks, and what enemies to prioritize killing first... then you're hooked.

This game doesn't require a PhD to beat--it's anything but a thinking man's game once you figure it all out, which doesn't take too long. But it is a very zen game. Once you're comfortable with everything the game's throwing at you, you'll enter a flow-state where you're mowing down hundreds of enemies and scraping by with a tad bit of health.

HD remake done right. Some of the best optimization and visual options you'll ever see in a PC game too, so you could get this thing running on a toaster if needs be. Great game.

Do you remember how the world was before Serious Sam? Don’t answer that; at this point, your reply is likely to make my ancient form crumble to dust and blow away in the wind. But there did exist a time before horde modes, before Painkiller, before nuts.wad, before the very concept of just giving players a giant gun and a room stuffed full of meaty enemies. Serious Sam was the quippy bastard that ushered us into a golden age of endless gibs, starting with a blood-and-buckshot-fueled romp through ancient Egypt. There have been several remakes of The First Encounter over the years, and HD has always been my weapon of choice for revisiting the genesis of the series. Fortunately, both the gameplay and the remake itself have aged plenty gracefully enough for the modern generation to get their fill of chaingun strafing and headless screaming.

Did you know these mad murderfests have a story? It’s true! In the far-flung future, Earth is on its last legs following an alien invasion spearheaded by the villainous Mental. Sam “Serious” Stone is the last protagonist left standing and the cornerstone of the Earth Defense Force, and they’ve got a plan for underdogging this war by sending Sam back in time to ancient Egypt. There, he’ll have to uncover the connections between the Egyptians and ancient aliens (yes, obviously, it was aliens) to summon a weapon that can change the course of history. Mental, however, is not about to let his conquest get re-written, and sends his massive, motley forces back to overrun the past. Good thing Sam is an expert in killing everything, everywhere, at all times, or that might be a problem!

This is one of those wonderful cases where someone had to write a ridiculously tenuous plot to connect an alien army, Egypt, and a guy running around in All Stars with a rocket launcher, and pulled it off to be built upon for decades. The meat of the game, of course, is turning ludicrous quantities of enemies into meaty chunks, and it does not fail to deliver. The classic Serious Sam experience is triggering a flood of enemies, then running backwards or wildly strafing while blazing away with lasers, bullets, and bombs until only you remain standing. The eclectic mix of foes keeps this interesting, as galloping skeletons, towering mechs, screeching harpies, and the now-ubiquitous screaming headless suicide bombers swarm Sam in varying volumes and formations.

What might surprise you, if you’re new to the series or coming to this one after future games, is how even-handed the earlier levels are. The front half of The First Encounter could almost be mistaken for a normal FPS, with reasonable enemy placements and moderate body counts. The scope of the levels, sprawling into the distant desert sands, still set it apart, and there are a few memorable setpiece battles that remind you what series it is you’re playing. But it’s clear that Serious Sam started as more of a balance between massive brawls and shorter encounters, something that later games moved away from as they fully embraced the madness that made Sam the man he is. The First Encounter is definitely more straight-forward, even in its big climactic late-game battles, than The Second Encounter is in its opening hour.

As for the remake itself, it’s certainly a faithful rendition of the absurd sorties and secrets that made up the original release. The (relatively) modern engine gives the game some much-needed fidelity that holds up great even now, though some of the building textures and geometry might give you pause if you stop to admire your surroundings too long. The UI is clean and the weapons look great, especially as they tear through hordes of enemies. This particular edition of The First Encounter loses a few of the more creative gravity-based rooms from the original, which is a definite shame, but does offer a few extra secrets in some levels that really benefit from them. Speaking of secrets, this is a series that really must be respected for both the hilarity and sheer volume of secrets it manages to cram in between arenas.

A full romp through ancient Egypt (the two secret levels included) will run you about six hours, which is a perfectly reasonable length of time to enjoy some Serious Sam. Anything longer than that, and you definitely risk burnout on Sam’s particular brand of FPS action. It’s honestly hard to argue that The First Encounter hasn’t aged gracefully, as it delivers on the promise of massive mayhem against previously unthinkable volumes of foes. A fair number of games have topped this one in size and spectacle (most of them subsequent Serious Sam games), but I find it comforting that the original, the game that showed us how much fun truly massive shootouts can be, is still as entertaining as it ever was.

Finished the game. I had never seen any gameplay or played a Serious Sam game before, so I went into it with no nostalgia whatsoever. As a completely new player, I genuinely enjoyed it, and I think it still holds up.

I chose Hard difficulty right from the start, and I’m glad I did. It was challenging at times, but never more than I could handle. If you’re new to this style of shooter, I’d recommend starting on Normal, or Hard if you want a proper challenge.

The basic formula is simple, fast, and chaotic, but it worked surprisingly well for me even without any previous attachment to the series. The Egyptian setting also works well and gives the game a clear identity, although I would have appreciated a bit more environmental variety.

My only other complaint is the Kleer Skeletons. Toward the end, the way they repeatedly leap at you from around corners became predictable and slightly annoying.

Was it worth the money? Yes. The fact that I enjoyed it as a first-time player with no nostalgia for it is probably the strongest compliment I can give it.

As a massive fan of old-school FPS, I've played a lot of them, and if I had to make a top 5 list of my favorites, Serious Sam would definitely be on that list. It has its own style of action based on intense ambushes with massive numbers of enemies in large open areas. And honestly, it's some of the best fun I've had playing a shooter.

The first two games (First and Second Encounter) are the gold standard for the series, with their blend of rock-solid gameplay, unrelenting action with a satisfying arsenal, and just the right amount of tongue-in-cheek silliness that pokes fun at the genre. And of course there's the memorable cast of enemies, including the beheaded kamikaze whose signature "AAAAAAA-" makes you panic as it gets closer and closer.

The difficulty is right on point as well. Because the enemies themselves have pretty straightforward AI, the game can compensate by throwing dozens of them at you at a time. And just because they're simplistic doesn't mean they're easy to deal with. Strafing, crowd control, and using the right weapon at the right time are key to surviving in Serious Sam.

On one last note, I would recommend getting the HD version over the regular one. While it is true that in the HD version could not replicate gravity mechanics due to the new engine, which neuters a couple of secrets and one section in Second Encounter, the truly stunning visuals and improved weapon-switching more than make up for it.

Bottom line: this game is an all-time classic and a blast in either single-player or co-op.

Mainstream video games have almost always followed the 'bigger is better' model. As the years pass, we want greater production values, bigger studios, more ambitious concepts, hundreds of VFX and modelling departments, celebrity voice actors and scriptwriters. Video games have replaced Hollywood, with GTA 5 earning more than $7B in profit - that's almost 3x the higher grossing movie of all time, Avengers: End Game.

To sustain this hunger, video games are becoming more and more pricey. Spyro 2 cost me £14.99 on release date in 1999. Now, the newest Modern Warfare 2 costs £59.99 (which doesn't even include all the multiplayer content - that costs extra). However, keeping up appearances is perhaps not all it's cracked up to be. The smash hit Dark Souls was produced up to 50% cheaper than its contemporaries, and to give an extreme example, the initial build of Minecraft only required 6 days of manpower to produce, ultimately becoming the highest selling game of all time.

Serious Sam's success is directly attributable to modest means. Appearing in 2001, the game released for $19.99 RRP in North America, challenging the established $49.99 price tags of its contemporaries and offering a budget friendly shooter. The concept of the game was straight-forward: no elaborate story, complicated scripts, Hollywood voice acting, or hundreds of side-quests. Instead, it aimed to do only a few things, but to do it well.

Serious Sam's gameplay revolves almost entirely around horde combat. This is the idea that there's a craft, almost a science, to overwhelming the players with extreme numbers of enemies while also keeping it fun, balanced and thoughtful The game pits you against hundreds of enemies (1,000+ across a whole level) and challenges you to move precisely and tactically eliminate certain threats first. 

For example, suicide bombers require urgent action and must be eliminated before they reach the player. However, what if there's a stampede of bulls running at you too? This forces the player to calculate the threat level of each enemy in accordance to the amount of potential damage they can cause you, as well as time you have available to react to each one. In this case, the suicide bombers may look the highest priority, but the stampede of bulls are bound to reach the player first. 

But what if a walker is added into the mix? It has a high damage output, but can be dodged relatively easily, as long as you have time to pay attention to its attacks. Do you? You might need to kill the suicide bombers first to give you time to think about that...

Movement is essential here, and for the most part it feels fast and responsive. Sam can jump and dodge incoming attacks and you don't have to worry about stamina. One slight is that switching weapons on a controller can be quite challenging due to the high number of weapons. The weapon wheel is awkward to use, and Serious Sam could learn much from Quake and GTA 5's weapon wheel system which is much more streamlined. This causes you to frantically scroll through weapons at times, putting you at a slight disadvantage in a game which is exceptionally difficult, even on the "normal" setting. 

However, if you hold your nerve you'll almost always get a thrilling and fair fight. Serious Sam looks absolutely gorgeous with superb lighting, texture detail and gore effects while offering a 100% rock solid 60FPS in all situations - impressive given the hundreds of enemies often on screen. Although some open environments feel a bit destitute, Serious Sam packs a lot of secrets into its low number of buildings and interiors and I found it genuinely challenging to seek them all out.

Overall Serious Sam, ironically for a game based around horde combat, simultaneously proves that less is more. It seems fitting that, 20 years later, the game is still finding its way into cheap festive sales (I bought the game for £2.19) while providing the same joy and challenge that it did for gamers back in 2001. This is a really easy game to recommend to FPS veterans and, if you can handle high difficulties, is an absolute blast to play.

Croteam makes a smash and they do it without any logic, realism, or sense. 

[b]The Campaign:[/b]
Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is an epic game which takes place in Ancient Egypt. This first person shooter is based in the future where the world is about to be destroyed by the monster Mental. All hope is lost until we discover that the way to defeat these monsters can be traced from our past. Further research reveals that humanity has discovered an ancient race the Sirians who had also fought and lost to Mental's might. Humanity finds the ancient Sirian technology known as the Time-Lock which can allow one person to traverse time and space. Our protagonist Sam, who may be very serious, is a champion, a hero, and a legend for humanity. Fighting off every alien he encounters to the end Sam, a true warrior, is given the ultimate task. To use the Time-Lock to travel back in time and to defeat Mental while he is busy dealing with the Sirians. 

[b]The Gameplay:[/b]
Serious Sam is revitalized in HD with a stunning thirteen levels (plus an additional two secret levels) digitally remastered and designed to meet the demand of modern day consumers. The graphics are not going to be anything like your blockbuster games, but that’s because the original was produced in 2001 and this is just a remastering. But the game looks rather clean and plays incredibly well. This game not only has secret levels, but is filled with little secrets for the avid gamer. Mysteries abound and things to find Serious Sam leaves you without want. 

[b]Result:[/b]
I played Serious Sam: The First Encounter only a little bit when it was released in 2001. Then purchased it recently because it was on sale. Not being an avid fan of the series I can definitely say this game is a fun purchase even if you never really played the original. There are an abundance of crazy enemies, a wacky story (that makes you keep wondering where all the humans are), awesome weapons, fun boss fights, and lots of crazy items. This game not only challenges you in combat making you feel like a hero, but also puts you to the test by throwing puzzles all over the place. The game requires you to solve puzzles, complete challenges, and defeat enemies in order to progress. The levels are long, the campaign is long, the game is a blast, it’s a must buy. If you like puzzles, you like first person shooters, you want nostalgia, or you just like to be a hero then this is the game for you.

Pros:
+Incredibly fast paced combat
+Puzzles in every level
+Secret levels and many secrets within each level.
+Lots of fun an interesting enemies
+An abundance of bosses
+Crazy amount of fun weapons to shoot about
+Digitally remastered and in 1080p
+Fun and gripping story that mixes reality with fantasy

Cons:
-There is a limit to the amount fo auto-saves, you will lose older auto-saves in order for new ones to save, but don't worry you can just continually make saves yourself (I had over 200 by the end of the campaign).
-The sensitivity can randomly spark (meaning it just shoots up and your character can suddenly turn with only the slightest mouse movement facing you the wrong way).

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is exactly what it promises to be: a classic old-school FPS built around fast movement, large enemy hordes and constant action. There is very little focus on narrative, progression systems or anything beyond the core objective of moving forward and surviving increasingly chaotic encounters.

The gameplay follows a formula that was extremely common during its era. You explore large maps, collect weapons and fight dozens of enemies at the same time while constantly staying on the move. The game rarely asks the player to do anything beyond shooting, dodging and adapting to larger enemy waves, but that simplicity is also part of its identity.

One aspect that surprised me is how the level design avoids excessive repetition. Many shooters from this period relied heavily on reusing environments and layouts, but throughout my time playing I rarely felt like I was running through the same locations over and over again. 

My biggest criticism is not necessarily directed at the game itself, but rather at how my own preferences have changed over the years. When I was younger, especially during the Windows XP era, I spent countless hours playing Serious Sam 2 and similar shooters. At the time, endless waves of enemies, simple objectives and pure action were enough to keep me entertained for entire afternoons.

Today, after playing hundreds of games across many different genres, I find it much harder to stay invested in a gameplay loop built almost entirely around arena combat and enemy hordes. The formula still works, and I can understand why so many players continue to enjoy it, but it no longer holds my attention the way it once did.

That does not make Serious Sam HD a bad game. On the contrary, it successfully delivers exactly the experience it was designed to provide. It knows what it wants to be and remains faithful to the identity that helped make the franchise popular in the first place.

In the end, Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a solid classic shooter that still captures the spirit of old-school FPS design. It may not have the same appeal for me that it had years ago, but I can still appreciate what it represents and why it earned such a strong reputation among fans of the genre.

The first two Serious Sam games were pretty novel when they were first released.  As Sam, players ran through massive levels, fighting similarly massive groups of (often massive) enemies.  It wasn't exactly the most radical idea on paper, but it was executed on a  [i]scale[/i] that was previously unheard of in FPS games.  Levels often had over a thousand enemies, with fights pitting hundreds of opponents against the player simultaneously; a few enemies were even larger than [i]entire maps[/i] in other FPS games.

Since then, several of the games Serious Sam has (inevitably) been compared to have caught up to Sam's scope--for instance, there are countless Doom "slaughter" WADs that will throw hundreds or thousands of enemies at you.  But whereas most of Doom's arsenal was never really intended to contend with thousands of enemies, Sam's was built from the ground up with mass extinction in mind, and its bestiary was designed for enormous arena battles.

Weapons are your primary means of interacting with the world in an FPS and, in the case of Serious Sam, the arsenal is especially rock solid.  You begin with the typical pistol(s) and combat knife, but it isn't long before you're fielding double-barreled shotguns, miniguns, laser rifles, and even an enormous cannon.  Virtually every firearm fills a niche and will find ample usage--especially on higher difficulties.  Rockets might travel further to snipe distant stationary targets, but the grenade launcher can charge up significantly faster projectiles and shoot around corners; the laser gun doles out tremendous damage up front, but its projectiles take time to travel through the air; the minigun's hitscan shots can mow down faraway crowds, but its ever-so-slight wind-up is a liability in close quarters.  

The guns generally feel great to use, as well.  With an appropriate thunderclap, the double-barreled shotgun reduces Kleer to bone fragments; the SBC Cannon's VW Bug-sized shots blast through enemies like so many bowling pins and wipe swathes of the battlefield clean.

Enemies are well-designed, too.  Unlike later installments in the Serious Sam series, TFE and TSE don't make the mistake of having numerous hitscan enemies.  Rather, most opponents produce a variety of physical projectiles--some follow you, some scatter, some cut through the air in small volleys, and some lazily fly towards their target--that can be [u]seen[/u] and [u]dodged[/u].  That one factor is crucial because it means that dodging can keep you alive even when fighting a hundred foes.  Indeed, Serious Sam almost feels like a sort of "bullethell"-FPS at times, and by encouraging fancy footwork over taking cover, the game maintains a higher degree of momentum than many modern FPS games.  The sheer variety of enemies can be a refreshing change of pace from the standard/heavy/sniper trifecta that so many FPS games like to focus on nowadays.

Then there are the levels:  They're huge, and they're especially gorgeous in the HD versions.  While TFE focuses exclusively on an Egyptian-themed mapset, it still includes some beautful setpieces including sprawling palaces, moody moonlit stretches, and Oases.  It certainly doesn't hold a candle to TSE's greater variety, but it does its best.  The maps are [i]packed[/i] full of secrets--some obvious and some devious--as well as easter eggs and entire hidden levels.  If you're a completionist, be prepared to spend a lot of time hunting down some of these secrets.

Given the size and scale of eveything, one of Serious Sam's biggest selling points is (perhaps unsurprsingly) its co-op support.  Up to 16 players can take on the campaign(s) in TFE and TSE, with a wide variety of player skins to choose from.  You've never really experienced everything a classic FPS has to offer until you're bunnyhopping across massive sand dunes, gunning down waves with half a dozen other players who look like cyborgs, neon cowboys, and Santa Claus.  In fact, there are several different co-op modes including a "Coin-Op Co-Op" arcade-style points/lives system that helps strike a nice balance between players having infinite lives and the level being over for a player the moment they die.  

Honestly, I played countless hours of the original TFE and TSE years ago and I still feel that I got my money's worth with the HD remakes.  While they run on earlier versions of the Serious Sam 3 engine than Serious Sam: BFE, they're still perfectly capable of squeezing out some fantastic graphics.  And if you're planning to run TFE HD on an older computer, the sheer number of graphics options will let you tweak everything until it's just right.

In conclusion, I'd happily recommend TFE HD to anybody who has enjoyed Serious Sam in the past, who is interested in taking a breather from modern FPS's, or who is simply interested in exploring what is now widely considered a "Classic FPS".

**Serious Sam: The First Encounter** is a legendary first-person shooter that set a benchmark for pure action gaming. Released in 2001, it throws players into the role of Sam "Serious" Stone, humanity's last hope against the alien overlord Mental. Set in stunning ancient Egyptian landscapes, the game pits you against waves of bizarre and deadly enemies, from headless kamikazes to towering biomechanical monstrosities.  

The gameplay focuses on unrelenting combat, with an arsenal of powerful weapons like the cannon and rocket launcher. Its clever level design and diverse enemy encounters keep the action intense and engaging. The blend of humor and over-the-top mayhem makes it a unique experience in the FPS genre.  

Though the story takes a backseat to the action, the game’s relentless pace and large-scale battles make it a cult classic. For fans of old-school shooters, it’s a must-play.

The original Serious Sam (SS1) is an okay game, but it's far from being among my favorite FPS games. The maps - but not the combat experiences - are fairly boring, have a monotonous theme, and do not encourage exploration as did 90s FPS titles based on the Doom and Build engines. SS1 more or less plays like Doom II would have played like IF Doom II had been an arcade game where the action is largely based on fighting waves of enemies in large arenas.

The main thing that spoils SS1 for me are the 'suicide bomber' enemies. They run after your character in waves and relentlessly scream from the time they see you until they detonate. The screaming is unnerving and you will continue to hear it in your head even once those particular enemies are no longer present.

One thing that this HD remaster of SS1 has going for it are its graphics. They look pretty good, and are seemingly well optimized. You might like the game play if you have a thing for FPS games that pit the player against literally dozens of enemies at once, and where the emphasis is on combat rather than exploration.

Speaking of enemies, a lot of them teleport (appear) out of thin air. It is seemingly impossible to sneak up on enemies, even though you have a melee weapon that would be ideal for such attacks.

In conclusion, SS1 is a competent FPS, but I'm not a fan of what it was trying to do. As someone who would much rather play old school FPS titles like Doom, Heretic, Strife, Rise of the Triad, Aliens Versus Predator, Duke Nukem 3D, and/or Quake, I do not recommend SS1. However, I wouldn't call it a 'bad' game. SS1 isn't my cup of tea, but I think I could have enjoyed it more if it had a greater variety of environments, and especially if exploration had been factored into the level design.

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a first-person shooter game developed by Croteam and published by Devolver Digital. It is a remastered version of the original Serious Sam game released in 2001, featuring updated graphics, improved sound, and other enhancements.

[h1]Short version: 87%[/h1]
For those who missed the awesomeness of the first Serious Sam games, the HD remake is the perfect spot to jump into this old-school FPS franchise of serious weaponry, hordes of aliens, corny humour, and most importantly: lots and lots of mindless but oh-so-fun action.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
After the not so enthusiastic reception of Serious Sam 2, CroTeam decided that it would be better if they returned the franchise to its roots. The result was Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter, which also marked the debut of third Serious Engine. (Apparently they wanted to erase the memory of SS2 so much that they released the remake before Serious Sam 3: BFE was finished.)

The finished product is mostly just a facelift on the original game, where the goal is still the same: use shotguns, rockets, cannons, and everything else in the vast arsenal to kill your way through a seemingly never-ending flood of monsters in ancient Egypt, all in order to stop an alien warlord called Mental before he eradicates humanity in the far future. All while finding silly little secrets and listening to the corniest one-liners any action hero ever spoken.
There are a few minor tweaks here and there: some new level secrets, rebalanced difficulty (easiest settings don’t reduce enemy health that much), and a few modified enemy spawn compositions or locations. They are not too large to make new players feel they don’t get the original experience, but enough to give something even for the veterans.

The graphical update is surprisingly humble. CroTeam touched the levels with respect, only making sure they were up to 2009’s standards, without adding unnecessary effects or any flashy things. This may come off as bad news for those who are used to FPS games being all about grandiose visuals and on-rails gameplay, but great news for those who want to know what makes these games so good but don’t want to go old-school in the graphical department.

Serious Sam HD: The First Encounter is a remake of Serious Sam: The First Encounter, as you could guess. It was released in 2009 by Croteam and was also known as the first game to use Serious Engine 3. And yep, as serious as ever.
It also came out on X360 through Xbox Live service. The only difference that I am aware of is that it had multiplayer only up to 4 players and aim assist.

Multiplayer community seems to be dead. Okay, maybe not completely, I did get into some match once at one day. But in other times server list is completely empty. And it makes sense, since Serious Sam HD: The Second Encounter has Fusion feature which means that owners of SSHD:TFE get to have Egypt levels to be ported into that game. So instead most of people play in SSHD:TSE.

Premise of original Serious Sam is that Sam Stone is sent into past into Egypt to try to stop the Mental forces before they destroy the Earth. And to do this he would need to pass many levels that have sections designed to serve as arenas to lock players inside. You didn't have as much exploration as in Doom or whatever Quake clone game. Instead it was more focused in pacing and tactical choices during combat itself, with encounters lasting few waves, as enemies keep pressuring you to move around. There were a lot of different enemy types and you had a lot of different specialized weapons, so you would have to choose correct gun for each sitatuation, prioritize targets and avoid all the different attacks. It's a classic!

HD is surprisingly faithful to the original. I kinda expected it to change a lot of core gameplay, but Croteam is just a honest indie company and gave a game just a nice graphics upgrade. Gameplay is almost same and the awesome soundtrack is completely identical. It's quite nice! And yep, even included Karnak from demo version, just like original. No technology test though.

And yea, it looks excellent, with much more natural looking desert and canyons. And if you take a careful look then you will see that some details that was just part of texture is now actual geometry, for example. Though, environment feels not fully finished, as inner places didn't get any additional details and some models seemed to have same textures quality, like statues, despite having more destruction phases. Just good nice new rendering with new light. Though I do wonder about some changes. For example, Alley of Spinxh levels is always at night and the third level of tomb has a fog changed from nice blue color to some dusty brown. As if Egypt doesn't have enough brown color with all sand.

But hey, look at all those great shiny weapons. And look at all the remade enemy models, now with ragdolls. Gore and weapons effects just got sexier, as you can now even gib part of enemies bodies, dismembering them, splitting apart, blowing head off with shotgun. It's awesome. Just look at the bull's death, where it would still slide around after being shot, leaving a trail of blood! And heavier enemies now can even be gibbed with a cannon, the heaviest weapon you have. The only strange thing is that Skeleton Kleers and Harpies are always gibbed upon death. For skeletons it looks good. But for harpies it looks strange, even gibs looks like just a few tiny chunks.

It also got some nice editing on gameplay. Some beheaded have a saw on their heads, giving them a melee attack. Bomberman looks fancy with that head on a spike, even. And heavy biomechanoids only shoot a single rocket when close to player, to let him have it easier, while it almost always was a certain death being very close to one in original. Kamikazes also seem to have smaller radius of explosion too. Flying gnaars seem to be more dangerous, not stopping when attacking. And weapons switch was made faster, which I approve. Though for some reason you can't walk anymore. Not that it ever was needed, just fancy.
If there is one thing I am most thankful the most is that new Netricsa messages notification is put somewhere to the side of a screen and doesn't grab your attention so you can ignore it easily. It was freaking annoying to be visually nagged by it everytime I killed each enemy types while playing custom maps in original.

Though, not everything is going perfect and some cuts had to be made. Most noticeably is that some of obscure engine features of Serious Engine 1 weren't implented in Serious Engine 3. Due to this, all the gravity-changing shenagians had to be cut. To be honest, I don't miss them too much, in Serious Sam 1 they were used only as funny thing in a bunch of a secrets, plus once non-secret usage in a secret level. It probably costed more time to reimplent them for something so small. I mean, at least when Croteam was making the first Serious Sam they had plans to make it much bigger game, with futurustic levels which would abuse gravity features. Once they cut it all to be Egypt-only, well, it was pretty much funky leftover.
It also doesn't have mirror and sliding surface, which I remember used only once.

They also seemed to screw up weapon balance slightly. You see, minigun was made to shoot two times slower, but each bullet does two times damage and is supposed to consume two ammo. But it only consumes one. Result: There is no more reason to use Thompson and you effectively have two times more ammo for minigun than in original. Oh well.
But hey, at least Laser gun isn't glitched in HD. It would sometimes start shooting only at half-speed in original. So flaw taken, flaw given.

And multiplayer is still awesome. Didn't get to cooperative, but I bet it's same spam, with same cutscene-skipping. And competetive part is awesome, still fast-paced. Although I noticed that rocket-jumping got nerfed and jumping off the slope doesn't give you additional height. But you are supposed to use knife to run fast and it still gets you in many places. And yep, still awesome arena-shooter which proves that you don't need some fancy strafejumping to be balanced and fast-paced.
Oh yea, and double shotgun in original was shooting at double speed. In HD it's same as in single-player/coop. Not sure what I think of it, but I think I like it this way. But maybe I need more experience with both ways.

Oh yea, and did you know that original The First Encounter was particulary embaressing due to having only a single DM level? Thankfully, HD added a bunch of them, even including Little Trouble from The Second Encounter. Hm, though HD multiplayer doesn't have scorematch mode, only fragmatch. But no one, absolutely no one, was playing scorematch in original anyway, so nah.

Overall, not perfect, but damn excellent HD remake with a bit of balance editing, untouched core gameplay, some environment upgrade and great gore system.
And yes, those who want to play Egypt levels in Serious Sam HD: The Second Encounter have to have this game purchased.

A lot of this review is based on my experience with the Classic version, [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561199101512747/recommended/41050/] which I reviewed here.[/url]

My greatest worry going into this HD version of the Classic game was that I'd discover there had been no reason to play the original at all. Fortunately or unfortunately, that is not the case and I'm glad to have tried both.

The updated look makes this game feel like a new experience worth playing: Dunes actually have a wave-like rise and fall! Bullets send up sprays of sand! Rock walls look like rough stone! If you like gore in games, there's now blood splashing across your view, with far more chunks and bits sticking around longer, and I love how enemies turn to ash.

On the other hand, the new HD textures do diminish some of the beautiful places from before, like the once-vibrant Moon Valley becoming a land of ordinary brown tones. Enemies are a little harder to find now because they appear to be smaller, though they do look great.

Another big change for this game is a new engine, and that's a mixed bag at best. Yes, the game runs well and Sam's walking animation looks far more natural if you like 3rd person view. But I actually got sad when I reached secret rooms that used to have gravity flips (especially the trippy 360 gravity room) and now don't, presumably because the new engine doesn't allow that. Same goes for other secrets such as the swinging bridge to Moon Valley.

After beating levels you can go back and replay them with interesting modifiers such as no health and armor items or infinite ammo. The full game on Tourist with infinite ammo for a rocket & cannon run is a fun ride that only takes a couple hours if you know where to go and what to do.

Giving enemies up to 400% their usual strength sounds on paper like multiplying enemy numbers by 11 which I loved in Serious Sam 2. In practice, this isn't much fun for the usual reasons that bullet sponge enemies in games are not fun, unless you enjoy putting a hard day's work into your gaming.

Of course we have achievements now too, and I like when these set challenges to extend game time such as playing without firing bullets or completing one hard level without needing to load. Thankfully the custom game options make some of these a lot nicer to complete.

But as someone who doesn't like online modes, the number of deathmatch achievements here is a special kind of pain. I love how there's a special mode for co-op and I have enjoyed deathmatch modes in other games with local friends, but not online and not for boring achievements.

Luckily some people still hang around to join random deathmatches, such as A__ and B__ who found me once on a full tour of deathmatch maps, and we can only hope there are veterans still willing to fly randos through the co-op game with the special parameters. 

Finally, I'll admit this feels like a weird complaint but I somehow expected more from the HD remaster, especially after playing Serious Sam 2 with their big dual wielding update. The co-op is great and the deathmatches work, but I expected ... the enemy multiplier from Serious Sam 2? The ability to change enemy appearances like some mods do? Perhaps a new bonus level? More, somehow.

In summary, play this game for the HD experience and co-op mode, but play the Classic version too.

It's funny: Serious Sam is an undisputed classic, and I enjoy it and would recommend it to any classic FPS fan, but it's a really fuckin' boring game. There's simply no way around how dissociating it feels mowing down hordes of enemies in vacant, visually uninteresting arenas... over and over again. 

The shooting feels solid enough, and movement is fast and responsive, but the game's readily apparent formula of throwing you into a box with a seemingly indefinite number of enemies gets old fast. It's just overkill. When Serious Sam initially released, sure, it was an impressive feat, but playing it nearly 20 years later with an updated skin job does little to remedy the more tedious aspects of the gameplay.

If you're a fan of classic FPS games, I'd still recommend this as a purchase, but with the caveat that you do so on sale, exclusively.

[Note: I haven't played the 2001 version, so I can't compare the two. I also played entirely on the Normal difficulty, and I understand that the experience is very different between difficulty settings.] 

TFE starts out pretty awkward. For one thing, the early selection of weapons (excluding secret weapons) is not great, thanks to a surprisingly anemic pair of shotguns (the Coach Gun may be double-barreled, but a Super Shotgun it ain't) and a rocket launcher that's mainly useful for direct hits rather than splash damage. And in the first few levels, enemies can spawn in or notice you almost at random, such that I often finished a big fight and then kept running into weak enemies that somehow didn't activate. This (along with the questionable choice to play battle music whenever an enemy is after you, not just during the main fights) creates a herky-jerk rhythm that always turned me off when I tried the game in the past.

But stick with it until maybe Level 5, and you'll really start to see the game's strong suit: fast-paced, intense fights where you can easily get overwhelmed by waves of enemies, most of whom will charge you instead of shooting from a distance. Without a beastly shotgun or a splashy rocket launcher, crowd control becomes much less simplistic and you really need to think about your methods to survive. It's very satisfying when you land on a good strategy for a particular encounter -- prioritizing the enemies that should die first, positioning yourself well to herd rushing enemies together and stay hidden from snipers, and using the right weapons for the job. Speaking of weapons, that aspect improves too, as the rocket launcher proves very worthy (albeit dull) and you come to realize that machine guns are to Serious Sam what shotguns are to many other Doom-like FPS. The rest of the arsenal is pretty fun too, especially the game's most powerful weapon, a unique and devastating piece whose full potential requires a bit of skill to realize...but I've made enough Doom references already.

The Normal difficulty is tougher than what I'd expect from a "Normal" setting, even by classic FPS standards -- on the one hand, I was adjusting to the game's unusual style of play, but in The Second Encounter I still found Normal almost as hard. That said, I think intensity is what these games are all about (well, also goofy Croatian humor) so if you just get acquainted with the F6 key and power through, you'll probably have more fun than you would on a lower difficulty. You might also consider watching others play if you can't get the hang of it. Personally I learned a lot from decino's videos on YouTube -- even though he played on Serious difficulty (and the non-HD version), which is miles away from Normal, it helped me understand the main flaws in my approach. I still struggled a lot in certain places, and almost gave up on the final boss because 
(arguably a minor spoiler but just read it) [spoiler]for no apparent reason, the game strongly implies that you can't hurt the boss by shooting it with your current weapons. In reality, the primary way of killing the boss is to shoot it. Like every other enemy.[/spoiler] But despite the moments of frustration, I really enjoyed it when the game pushed me to the edge of my mediocre abilities and I still got by.

If you like this game at all, check out The Second Encounter, as it adds some great new weapons and enemies, and is set in 3 different locations instead of one. I personally like it a lot more. Unfortunately it ramps up the difficulty very quickly, so you should either start with TFE or play TSE on one of the lower settings.

[h1] Serious Sam: The First Encounter — thanks for the childhood, but I’m not gonna play it now [/h1]

Bought it out of nostalgia. I remember as a kid talking with the boys about those headless kamikazes and skeletons with grenade launchers, arguing who was cooler — Sam or Duke. We took turns playing, laughed our asses off when he got torn to pieces. But I never finished it — not back then, not now.

Launched it recently. The graphics are cubes, enemies come at you in hordes, and after half an hour my head hurts. It’s suffocating, clunky, and those hordes are more annoying than anything. I get that I won’t finish it and won’t replay it.

But still, thanks. Not for the gameplay, but for those memories, for the talks with friends, for summer and childhood. Sam, you’re not the best game, but you’re part of my life. I’ll keep you in my memory the way you were.
